title: Strengthening NSW fuel security through the Investment Delivery Authority
description:
Alongside the EOI round, the NSW Government will run a Market Sounding process to help understand what’s needed to unlock future investment related to fuel security.
To further improve fuel security, the Minns Labor Government will also expand the Renewable Fuel Scheme to include low-carbon and renewable liquid fuels.
The NSW Government will add renewable liquid fuels such as sustainable aviation fuel, renewable diesel and biodiesel.
Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said: “Strengthening fuel security isn’t just an energy issue, it’s a cost‑of‑living issue for households and businesses across the state.
“This targeted fuel security round is about identifying serious, large‑scale projects that can make a real difference to how resilient our fuel supply is in NSW.
text:
Ongoing instability in the Middle East has highlighted the risks of heavy reliance on imported fuels and long, exposed supply chains. This reinforces the need for NSW to build stronger domestic fuel capability.

The targeted IDA round will focus on commercial-scale projects valued at $100 million or more that would directly improve fuel security, including:

fuel storage and distribution infrastructure

domestic, import‑independent liquid fuel production, focused on renewable fuels and their feedstocks such as sustainable aviation fuel, renewable diesel, biodiesel, biomethane and green ammonia

heavy electric vehicle charging hubs and fleets, to reduce reliance on diesel over time.

The IDA will use its existing operating model to help remove delivery barriers, coordinate engagement across government and support endorsed projects to progress more quickly.

Alongside the EOI round, the NSW Government will run a Market Sounding process to help understand what’s needed to unlock future investment related to fuel security.

This will provide an option for proponents whose projects do not yet meet IDA EOI criteria, such as those at an earlier stage of development, to still put forward information about potential projects as part of the fuel security round.

Ultimately, this is about protecting households, businesses and essential services from future fuel disruptions, supporting regional jobs, and making NSW better prepared for global shocks beyond our control.

To further improve fuel security, the Minns Labor Government will also expand the Renewable Fuel Scheme to include low-carbon and renewable liquid fuels.

The Scheme already provides financial incentives for green hydrogen and will shortly be expanded to include biomethane. The NSW Government will add renewable liquid fuels such as sustainable aviation fuel, renewable diesel and biodiesel.

In addition to boosting fuel security, these renewable liquids can help cut emissions in harder-to-electrify industries such as aviation, freight and heavy transport, while driving economic growth and job opportunities.

The NSW Government will consult industry on the changes, which are designed to give investors confidence and unlock private and Commonwealth co-investment.

The fuel security round of the IDA and the Market Sounding process will open on 1 June, 2026 and industry will have three weeks to submit their projects.

For more information on the IDA visit www.nsw.gov.au/departments-and-agencies/investment-nsw/investment-delivery-authority.

Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said:

“Strengthening fuel security isn’t just an energy issue, it’s a cost‑of‑living issue for households and businesses across the state.

“This is about making sure NSW is better prepared, better protected and better positioned to deal with global shocks, while keeping our economy and essential services moving.

“We also recognise that not every good idea is ready to go on day one, which is why we’re running a market sounding process alongside the EOI round.”

Minister for Planning and Public Spaces Paul Scully said:

“The impact of the recent fuel supply challenges has been felt across a vast array of industries, hitting the back pockets of everyone in NSW.

“There is great port and industrial land capacity in NSW that could be harnessed to support our long-term fuel security while helping reduce transport emissions at the same time.

“This new targeted round of the Investment Delivery Authority will make sure NSW attracts the right investments to create a more resilient fuel future.”

Minister for Industry and Trade Anoulack Chanthivong said:

“The Minns Labor Government has the right plan to shore up fuel supply, availability and price transparency for motorists in every corner of NSW.

“The Investment Delivery Authority is designed to help major, strategically important projects cut through complexity and get moving faster.

“This targeted fuel security round is about identifying serious, large‑scale projects that can make a real difference to how resilient our fuel supply is in NSW.

“By running a focused Expression of Interest round, we’re sending a clear signal to industry that NSW is ready to work with proponents who are prepared to invest and deliver.”

text:
Tightening UK and EU sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) mandates are exposing a growing disconnect between regulatory targets and commercial reality, as production costs, feedstock limitations and scaling challenges continue to restrict viable SAF supply despite rising compliance demand.

SAF adoption remains primarily compliance-driven because prices are still significantly above conventional jet fuel. Industry leaders argue that widespread uptake will only occur once synthetic SAF approaches fossil fuel cost parity, enabling airlines to shift from tactical purchasing to long-term procurement strategies.

The industry’s main bottleneck is currently economic rather than technical or logistical, with high hydrogen production costs preventing large-scale investment. Innovations such as geothermal-powered synthetic fuel production could materially reduce costs, while also strengthening European energy security by reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels and volatile crude markets.

The tightening of sustainable aviation fuel mandates across the UK and EU is exposing a familiar industrial tension: regulatory ambition is accelerating faster than underlying production economics. Airlines are being compelled to decarbonise within defined timelines, yet the physical availability of SAF remains constrained by cost structures that have yet to reach investable thresholds. Recent warnings around tightening jet fuel supply in parts of Europe further sharpen the issue, underscoring how fragile fuel availability can be when supply chains are stretched and capital deployment lags policy signals.

At present, the SAF ecosystem is characterised less by technological immaturity than by economic misalignment. Feedstock limitations, high conversion costs and fragmented scaling pathways have combined to create a market where compliance demand outpaces commercially viable supply. The result is a widening gap between mandated volumes and achievable production.

“The only blockage is fuel unit economics, everything else is just noise,” Dan Sutton, CEO of Syntholene. “Mandate success, voluntary airline consumption, and industrial scale-up of SAF production infrastructure all hang on a step-change reduction in unit economic costs, with a path to cost competition with fossil fuels.

“Ultimately, as long as cleaner fuels cost three to ten times as much as fossil fuels, they will never be widely adopted. This constrains the ambition of industrial investors to bank the infrastructure necessary to increase production capacity to mandated levels.”

Price parity and procurement transformation

SAF today remains largely a compliance-driven purchase, treated as a regulatory obligation rather than a core input. For that dynamic to shift, pricing must converge decisively with conventional jet fuel. Without that inflection, airlines will continue to manage SAF exposure tactically rather than strategically, limiting long-term contracting and slowing the development of stable demand signals required for scale.

Emerging synthetic pathways, however, are beginning to challenge this status quo. If cost curves continue downward, SAF could transition into a mainstream procurement category, reshaping airline fuel strategies.

“Airlines will shift from compliance-driven purchases to core procurement once eSAF converges toward fossil parity, which we model in a carbon-priced environment aligned with the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS). For synthetic pathways to reach this inflection point, the factory gate price must realistically drop toward the €1.50 per litre range at small scale, and cost parity at industrial scale,” Sutton stated. “At this price, efuel producers can also offer long term price stability, decoupled from volatile feedstocks such as fossil and bio-inputs.

“Syntholene’s strategy is to drive hydrogen costs down to enable this shift, ensuring fuels meet ASTM D7566 standards for drop-in compatibility. Until synthetic fuels are materially cheaper than current experimental batches, they will remain a compliance burden rather than a strategic asset.”

From economics to scale: the shifting bottleneck

In the near term, the SAF constraint is overwhelmingly economic rather than logistical. Infrastructure, distribution networks and airline compatibility are largely in place, but projects struggle to reach Final Investment Decision due to uncompetitive production costs. This has effectively stalled the transition from pilot-scale innovation to industrial deployment.

Looking ahead five to ten years, the constraint is expected to shift. Once cost competitiveness is demonstrated at scale, capital markets are likely to respond rapidly, unlocking large-scale infrastructure investment. At that point, the industry challenge will pivot from proving viability to executing expansion at speed, with capacity build-out becoming the dominant concern.

“The fundamental bottleneck for the next five years is unequivocally an economics problem. Specifically, the thermodynamically constrained cost of low temperature hydrogen electrolysis does not achieve the unit economics necessary to compete with fossil fuel at any economy of scale,” Sutton explained. “Syntholene can increasingly demonstrate that we solve the cost problem through thermal integration, we anticipate the binding constraint will shift toward scaling production capacity to meet global 2030 targets. The transition depends on moving from lab-scale validation through demonstration facility and on to industrial-scale capital deployment.”

Process innovation and the cost curve reset

A critical, and often underappreciated, variable in SAF economics is process heat. Conventional eSAF pathways rely heavily on electricity-intensive hydrogen production, which drives up costs and limits efficiency.

This is where new production models are beginning to alter the cost landscape. Syntholene’s geothermal-powered facility in Iceland, using a thermal hybrid approach, exemplifies how process innovation can directly reshape unit economics. By reducing reliance on high-cost electricity and improving utilisation rates, such models aim to deliver step-change reductions in production cost, reportedly up to 70 percent versus incumbent approaches.

“Process heat is the key that fundamentally unlocks the physics of the cost curve. By substituting high-cost renewable electricity with high-enthalpy geothermal heat, Syntholene reduces the electrical intensity of hydrogen production by 30-40 percent,” Sutton laid out. “This thermal hybrid model allows also us to operate at a baseload capacity factor of >90 percent when coupled to geothermal or nuclear heat sources, solving the intermittency challenges typical of standalone wind or solar systems. This integration is the structural differentiator that enables sub-US$2/kg hydrogen, and ultimately the path to sub-US$1/kg.”

Resilience and market reconfiguration

As Europe grapples with tightening jet fuel supply and ongoing exposure to import volatility, SAF, particularly synthetic variants, is increasingly being framed not just as a decarbonisation tool but as a strategic asset for energy security. Localised production models offer the potential to decouple aviation fuel supply from geopolitically sensitive crude markets, introducing long-term stability into airline operations.

If synthetic fuels achieve sustained cost competitiveness, the implications extend further. Capital is likely to migrate away from feedstock-constrained bio-based pathways towards scalable, resource-flexible synthetic solutions. In parallel, airline balance sheets could begin to treat SAF as both a hedge and a structural operating component, fundamentally altering procurement, contracting and risk management strategies.

“Synthetic fuels are as much about energy sovereignty as they are about emissions reduction, particularly as Europe seeks to reduce its deep and continuing dependence on fossil fuel imports. Localised eSAF production uncouples airlines from the geopolitical volatility of the crude oil supply chain, and offers long-term price stability attached to regional and friendly energy resources,” Sutton expressed.

text:
FlyORO Technologies Pte. Ltd. and Aether Fuels have signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding (MoU) to jointly explore the development of a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) supply chain, blending and related activities in support of Aether’s Project Beacon and future Aether SAF projects.

Both companies are headquartered in Singapore, with Aether Fuels also maintaining offices in Chicago, Illinois, U.S.A.

At the centre of the collaboration is Project Beacon, Aether’s planned commercial demonstration facility at Aster Pulau Bukom refinery in Singapore. Aether describes Project Beacon as the first next-generation, commercial-scale SAF production facility in Southeast Asia. The facility is designed to use the Aether Aurora technology platform to convert industrial waste gas and biomethane into Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA)-certified SAF, with expected output of up to 50 barrels of fuel per day, or approximately 2,000 tonnes per year. Lifecycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reductions are anticipated to exceed 70% versus conventional jet fuel. Construction is expected to start in 2026, with commercial operations targeted for 2028.

Through the MoU, the parties will evaluate how a next-generation SAF production pathway can be paired with flexible blending, storage interface, certification workflow, logistics and downstream market-delivery models. The collaboration is intended to accelerate operational readiness and commercial adoption while supporting Singapore’s role as a leading hub for aviation, innovation and sustainable industrial development.

FlyORO’s role in the collaboration centres on downstream enablement. The company will contribute its modular blending expertise to assess how flexible, on-demand blending could complement Project Beacon and future Aether projects. FlyORO’s AlphaLite system — first launched in Singapore as the world’s first modular SAF blending system — is designed to integrate with existing fuel infrastructure and enable scalable, site-deployable blending capability closer to the point of use. The platform draws on operational experience from FlyORO’s 2025 deployment with Wagner Sustainable Fuels and Boeing at Toowoomba Wellcamp Airport in Queensland, Australia.

Chief Executive Officer of FlyORO Technologies Jonathan Yeo said Singapore is one of the few markets where advanced fuel production, airport demand, logistics capability and policy momentum can come together at meaningful speed. He said through this MoU, the companies aim to explore how smarter downstream infrastructure can complement next-generation SAF production and help make supply more flexible, transparent and practical for the local market.

Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Aether Fuels Conor Madigan said Project Beacon is intended to demonstrate Aether’s breakthrough Aurora technology in commercial operation and unlock new and more abundant waste carbon feedstocks for SAF production. Madigan said working with FlyORO on this project gives the company an opportunity to evaluate how downstream blending and supply-chain innovation can support commercialisation in Singapore and accelerate overall SAF industry development.

The MoU is non-binding and non-exclusive. Any future collaboration remains subject to further technical, commercial, regulatory and definitive-agreement discussions between the parties.

description:

text:
Some shipowners are contracting green methanol supply that does not yet exist, potentially to avoid a future scramble for the fuel.

Wallenius Wilhelmsen will begin receiving bio-methanol bunkers from Equinor at the ports of Zeebrugge and Antwerp later this year, with a two-year supply agreement already in place. The Norwegian vehicle carrier has at least 14 methanol dual-fuel vessels on order for delivery between 2026-2028.

German carrier Hapag-Lloyd has signed an offtake with China’s Goldwind for 250,000 mt/year of green methanol, with deliveries expected to begin this year.

Fuels exist. The ships are coming. The deals are live. But not all agreements signed this year look like this.

In some cases, fuel supply is being secured years before either the vessels or production plants are operational.

London-based RFOcean has signed a binding long-term offtake agreement with ETFuels to purchase e-methanol at a fixed price from 2030. The fuel will come from ETFuels’ Rattlesnake Gap project in West Texas, a planned 120,000 mt/year facility currently at the front-end engineering and design stage. RFOcean’s eight methanol-ready vessels on order will not run on methanol upon delivery, but they are designed to be retrofitted later.

ETFuels has secured access to renewable power and biogenic CO2 for the plant, and confirmed incentives of around $1.5 billion under the US Inflation Reduction Act. With the offtake agreement in place, ETFuels said the project has moved into “financeable territory.”

“This agreement converts that fleet optionality into secured, fixed-price compliant fuel supply before the market tightens,” ETFuels said.

The producer added that the agreement was partly driven by FuelEU Maritime’s tightening greenhouse gas (GHG) intensity requirements from 2030, which are expected to increase demand for compliant fuels.

“This isn’t just about compliance, it’s about competitive positioning,” RFOcean’s chief executive Fredrik Rye-Florentz said.

“We believe compliant fuel will be scarce. By locking in supply now at fixed prices, we can offer our customers certainty and be in the forefront of a development which makes commercial sense today.”

In other cases, shipowners appear to be positioning more cautiously.

Hapag-Lloyd has also agreed a framework with Southern Energy Renewables for a potential long-term bio-methanol offtake from the producer’s planned plant in St. Charles Parish, Louisiana. A final investment decision is planned for 2027, with pilot production targeted for 2029 and initial production capacity of 220,000 mt/year by 2031.

Hapag-Lloyd has eight methanol dual-fuel containerships on order for delivery between 2028-2029 and is retrofitting five existing vessels for methanol propulsion.

Singapore-based X-Press Feeders has agreed a letter of intent to purchase up to 15,000 mt/year of bio-methanol from UK start-up PuriFire Energy.

The fuel is expected to come from planned facilities and co-developed port-based production sites across the UK and mainland Europe. PuriFire currently operates a research and development facility in Royston and a demonstration plant at Shoreham Port, but has not disclosed a production timeline or formal supply terms.

X-Press Feeders currently operates four methanol dual-fuel vessels and has at least another 10 on order.

Both agreements remain conditional on project milestones being met, but the willingness to engage before production starts suggests some shipowners see risk in waiting.

Developing an e-methanol project takes around two years, followed by another 2-3 years for construction, Yann Dumont, chief executive of Spanish project developer Reolum, told ENGINE.

With relatively few projects currently under development, available supply could tighten sharply as FuelEU Maritime’s GHG intensity limits begin to bite from 2030.

Competition for that supply will not come from shipping alone.

“SAF [sustainable aviation fuel] demand is coming along with maritime and others,” Dumont said.

Some shipowners are signing now to get ahead of that pressure. “These are strategical deals and some shipowners have understood it,” Dumont said.

Reolum’s first e-methanol plant, in Spain’s La Robla, is on track to begin biomass power operations in the fourth quarter of 2027, with methanol production to ramp up in the first half of 2028. Two further plants, in Villadangos and Monfarracinos, are scheduled to follow.

But not all developers have made it that far.

Swedish e-methanol developer Liquid Wind declared bankruptcy on 11 May, four days after submitting an environmental permit application for a large-scale plant in Örnsköldsvik. In a 2025 interview with ENGINE, chief executive Claes Fredriksson had said securing offtake agreements was critical before a project could move forward.

“It’s only when we have those offtakers that we can confidently develop a plant, or find an investor willing to finance it, and secure the necessary power…” he said.

“We can prepare a lot beforehand, but once we start building a plant, everything needs to be lined up.”

In other alternative fuels news this week, Busan Port Authority is planning to develop LNG and methanol bunker infrastructure at the port by 2032. The project includes the construction of a 370,000 cbm LNG storage tank and a 150,000 cbm methanol storage tank, the port authority said. It will also include a berth capable of accommodating vessels with capacities of up to 123,000 cbm, it added.

Molgas-owned bunker supplier Titan Clean Fuels has chartered a new LNG bunker vessel for physical deliveries in Zeebrugge and the wider ARA hub. The 8,000 cbm-capacity vessel, United LNG I, is owned by Luxembourg-based inland shipping firm Somtralux and operated by Belgian supplier United Bunkers.

title: Biofuel Bunker Snapshot: B30 prices gain in Rotterdam and Singapore
description:
Rotterdam and Europe Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO (POMEME) price has increased by $28/mt since Monday.
Prima Markets’ assessed POMEME barge price has registered a small gain of around $4/mt over the same period.
That could partially explain the increase in Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO (POMEME) price this week.
But Gibraltar’s price is at a narrow $10/mt premium over Lisbon’s B30-VLSFO price.
Singapore Singapore’s B30-VLSFO (UCOME) price has gained considerably during the week.
text:
Rotterdam and Europe

Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO (POMEME) price has increased by $28/mt since Monday.

Conversely, the port’s conventional VLSFO price has remained steady during the week. Prima Markets’ assessed POMEME barge price has registered a small gain of around $4/mt over the same period.

Bunker suppliers delivering low-carbon advanced biofuel blends in Dutch ports can generate ZRE A tickets, which can, for example, be sold to conventional fuel suppliers. This helps subsidise the price in Dutch ports compared to other ports.

The price of these ZRE A tickets fell from €125/mtCO2e ($145/mtCO2e) to €115/mtCO2e ($134/mtCO2e) during the week, according to Prima Markets. Prima said prices have been falling lately and that the ZRE market is still small, with only a limited number of participants contributing to price discovery.

But falling ticket prices could indicate an oversupplied market, where demand for biofuel is stronger than compliance demand for the certificates it helps generate. That could partially explain the increase in Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO (POMEME) price this week.

Rotterdam’s B30-LSMGO (POMEME) price has remained rather steady over the week, despite a $24/mt fall in the Dutch port’s conventional LSMGO price.

Rotterdam’s B30-LSMGO (POMEME) blend offers a steep $119/mt price discount to Lisbon’s B30-LSMGO.

Gibraltar’s B30-VLSFO (UCOME) price has edged $9/mt higher on the week. Its price premium over Rotterdam’s POMEME blend has dropped by $19/mt to $62/mt. But Gibraltar’s price is at a narrow $10/mt premium over Lisbon’s B30-VLSFO price.

Singapore

Singapore’s B30-VLSFO (UCOME) price has gained considerably during the week. The gain has been supported by a $49/mt rise in the port’s conventional VLSFO price.

Prima’s China UCOME cargo price has dropped $15/mt over the same period. Chinese UCOME is a key feedstock for Singapore’s B30-VLSFO blend.

Spot bunker demand for biofuel blends is very low in Singapore, a trader told ENGINE.

In other news from this week, logistics firm Kuehne+Nagel will claim nearly 3,000 mt of CO2-equivalent greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reductions from Hapag-Lloyd’s use of biofuel under a new book-and-claim agreement between the two companies. ENGINE’s analysis found the deal would contribute very modestly to Kuehne+Nagel’s Scope 3 emission cuts.

MSC Cruises has tested pure hydrogenated vegetable oil (HVO100) on one of its cruise ships. The fuel was produced from waste-based feedstocks, including used cooking oil (UCO), animal fats and agricultural residues. It was produced at biorefineries in Venice and Gela owned by Enilive, a subsidiary of Italian energy company Eni.

text:
Yield10 Bioscience has moved into a critical phase after the agtech company disclosed a Nasdaq delisting notice and initiated a strategic review, while at the same time warning that its current cash resources may not be sufficient to fund operations for the next twelve months, according to a company update published on 04/08/2024 and a subsequent filing referenced by Nasdaq in April 2024Yield10 Bioscience investor update as of 04/08/2024Nasdaq filings overview as of 04/15/2024.

As of: 17.05.2026

By the editorial team – specialized in equity coverage.

Yield10 Bioscience: core business model

Yield10 Bioscience focuses on the development of specialty oilseed crops, primarily based on Camelina sativa, with the aim of producing feedstocks for biofuels, sustainable aviation fuel and other biobased products. The company positions Camelina as a platform crop that can be engineered for higher oil content and improved agronomic traits, targeting both energy and nutritional marketsYield10 Bioscience company profile as of 03/01/2024.

The business model is built around trait development, seed production and potential licensing agreements with larger seed and energy companies. Yield10 Bioscience has historically generated limited revenue, with most income coming from research funding and early-stage collaborations rather than large-scale commercial seed sales. This makes the company highly dependent on external capital and partnerships to advance its technology pipelineYield10 Bioscience Form 10-K 2023 as of 04/08/2024.

For retail investors in the United States, Yield10 Bioscience represents a niche play in the broader clean energy and agtech ecosystem. The company aims to impact the US biofuel and sustainable aviation fuel value chains by supplying high-oil Camelina as a low-carbon feedstock. However, the early-stage nature of the business and the lack of predictable cash flows mean that the stock is typically followed by investors with a high risk tolerance and a long-term view on technology adoption.

Main revenue and product drivers for Yield10 Bioscience

Yield10 Bioscience’s potential revenue streams are tied closely to the commercial success of its Camelina-based technologies. The company works on traits that increase seed oil content, improve drought tolerance and raise overall yield, with the goal of making Camelina a competitive rotation or cover crop for farmers in North America and Europe. Licensing such traits to established seed companies or producing seed under contract could form the basis of future revenue if field performance and regulatory approvals alignYield10 Bioscience Form 10-K 2023 as of 04/08/2024.

Another key driver lies in potential offtake relationships with biofuel refiners and energy companies that seek low-carbon feedstocks. Yield10 Bioscience has previously highlighted the role of Camelina-derived oil in renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel value chains. If such offtake or joint development agreements are expanded, they could create a pathway from R&D to commercial-scale planting and processing, which in turn might support more stable revenue generationYield10 Bioscience news overview as of 03/15/2024.

In the near term, however, reported figures demonstrate that Yield10 Bioscience remains pre-commercial. In its Form 10-K for the year ended 12/31/2023, filed on 04/08/2024, the company reported only modest revenue while posting a net loss and negative operating cash flow, underlining the reliance on equity issuance or strategic transactions to fund ongoing operationsYield10 Bioscience Form 10-K 2023 as of 04/08/2024.

Industry trends and competitive position

The broader backdrop for Yield10 Bioscience is the global push toward lower-carbon fuels and more sustainable agricultural systems. In the United States, policy initiatives such as the Renewable Fuel Standard and various state-level low carbon fuel standards have created incentives for biofuel feedstocks with favorable greenhouse gas profiles. Oilseed crops that can be grown on marginal land or as cover crops are of particular interest because they can contribute to decarbonization without directly displacing food productionU.S. EIA biofuels overview as of 02/29/2024.

Camelina-based concepts compete not only with traditional oilseeds such as soybean and canola, but also with waste oils, tallow and other advanced feedstocks. Larger agribusiness and seed companies, as well as integrated energy majors, are investing in their own feedstock solutions, which can make it challenging for a small company like Yield10 Bioscience to secure a durable competitive position. Partnerships, technology differentiation and the ability to demonstrate robust field results therefore play a central role in the company’s strategyYield10 Bioscience news overview as of 03/15/2024.

From a capital markets perspective, the agtech and clean fuel sectors have experienced cycles of strong investor interest followed by periods of consolidation and funding constraints. For US retail investors, Yield10 Bioscience is situated within this volatile segment, where share prices can react sharply to regulatory headlines, partnership announcements or financing transactions. Liquidity on Nasdaq may be relatively limited compared with larger biofuel or seed companies, which can amplify price swings both to the upside and downside.

Why Yield10 Bioscience matters for US investors

Despite its small size, Yield10 Bioscience can be relevant for US-based investors looking to gain exposure to early-stage innovations at the intersection of agriculture and energy transition. The company’s focus on developing Camelina traits tailored to renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel aligns with policy priorities in the United States aimed at reducing emissions from hard-to-abate sectors like aviation. If such technologies progress successfully, they could contribute to domestic supply chains for low-carbon fuelsU.S. DOT sustainable aviation fuel overview as of 01/30/2024.

At the same time, the company’s disclosures about its limited cash runway and the Nasdaq delisting notice underscore the financial and listing risks that US investors must weigh. According to its Form 10-K for 2023, filed on 04/08/2024, Yield10 Bioscience indicated substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern without additional funding, highlighting the possibility of equity dilution, asset sales or other strategic alternativesYield10 Bioscience Form 10-K 2023 as of 04/08/2024.

For diversified portfolios, a stock like Yield10 Bioscience typically represents a speculative satellite position rather than a core holding. US investors who follow the stock often monitor catalysts such as strategic transactions, new field trial data, regulatory progress for engineered crops and developments in federal or state biofuel incentives. Each of these factors can influence market perception of the company’s prospects, even though the underlying financials currently reflect an early-stage R&D profile.

What type of investor might consider Yield10 Bioscience – and who should be cautious?

Yield10 Bioscience is generally aligned with investors who are comfortable with high volatility, extended development timelines and binary outcomes around funding or strategic deals. These market participants may be drawn to the potential upside associated with successful commercialization of proprietary crop traits and the possibility of partnerships with larger industry players. They typically accept that revenues may remain modest for several years while research and field work continueYield10 Bioscience Form 10-K 2023 as of 04/08/2024.

By contrast, more conservative investors who prioritize stable earnings, dividends and transparent cash flows may find the risk profile of Yield10 Bioscience less suitable. The going-concern warning, the Nasdaq compliance issues and the dependence on external capital all increase uncertainty about the long-term outcome for existing shareholders. For such investors, larger and more diversified companies in the agricultural or energy sectors may better match traditional risk and return expectations.

In addition, short investment horizons may not align well with the regulatory and agronomic cycles involved in crop trait development. Regulatory approvals for genetically engineered traits, multi-season field trials and the build-out of supply chains from seed producers to refiners all require time. Investors who focus mainly on near-term share price performance in this context face an elevated risk that key milestones take longer than anticipated or that additional capital raises alter the equity story.

Risks and open questions

The central risk for Yield10 Bioscience at the current stage is funding. As disclosed in the Form 10-K for the year ended 12/31/2023, filed on 04/08/2024, management stated that existing cash and cash equivalents were not expected to support operations for a full year, and that additional capital or strategic arrangements would be required. This situation introduces uncertainty about the structure and timing of future financing, including the potential for dilution or other measures that affect current shareholdersYield10 Bioscience Form 10-K 2023 as of 04/08/2024.

The Nasdaq delisting notice presents an additional layer of risk. If the company does not regain compliance with the exchange’s listing requirements, trading in the shares could move to an over-the-counter venue, which may reduce liquidity and alter how institutional investors view the stock. The company has indicated that it is evaluating options and pursuing a strategic review, but the outcome of these efforts remains uncertain as of the latest public filingsNasdaq filings overview as of 04/15/2024.

Operationally, questions remain around the pace at which Camelina-based traits can move from experimental plots to large-scale cultivation. Agronomic performance across different climates, farmer adoption economics and downstream processing capacity all influence the commercial trajectory. Any setbacks in field results, regulatory approvals or partner engagement could delay commercialization further, keeping revenue at low levels while expenses for R&D and regulatory work continue.

Conclusion

Yield10 Bioscience sits at a crossroads where its long-term vision of enabling low-carbon fuels through Camelina-based crops meets the immediate realities of funding pressure and listing risk. Public filings from April 2024 emphasize both the technological ambitions and the financial constraints, including a going-concern warning and a Nasdaq delisting notice. For US retail investors, the stock illustrates the opportunities and challenges embedded in early-stage agtech: potential exposure to structural energy-transition trends on one hand, and a heightened sensitivity to financing terms, regulatory progress and strategic decisions on the other. A balanced assessment therefore needs to weigh the company’s scientific and partnership prospects against its constrained balance sheet, limited revenue base and the possibility of further corporate restructuring or dilution.

title: Von 50 auf weniger als fünf: Klimainitiativen bei Airlines brechen um 96 Prozent ein
description:
Das zeigt sich nicht nur in der Wahrnehmung, sondern auch in Zahlen: Nachhaltigkeitsfonds verzeichneten zuletzt drei Jahre in Folge Mittelabflüsse.
Icao erfasst keine Nachhaltigkeitsinitiativen mehr Parallel dazu sprechen auch Unternehmen seltener über Themen wie Dekarbonisierung oder ESG.
Laut der International Civil Aviation Organization Icao ist die Zahl konkreter Initiativen von Airlines zur Reduktion von CO₂-Emissionen massiv gesunken, um ganze 96 Prozent.
Auch ein Zwischenziel, bis 2030 einen Anteil von 10 Prozent nachhaltigem Treibstoff zu erreichen, verschwand aus der Kommunikation.

text:
Die Gespräche ums Thema Klima sind leiser geworden. In Konferenzprogrammen, in Geschäftsberichten, in Investorengesprächen - vieles dreht sich heute um andere Schlagworte. Vor allem um Künstliche Intelligenz. Doch was bedeutet dieser Stimmungswandel für die Luftfahrt?

Noch vor wenigen Jahren war Klimaschutz eines der dominierenden Themen. Inzwischen ist die öffentliche Aufmerksamkeit deutlich zurückgegangen. Das zeigt sich nicht nur in der Wahrnehmung, sondern auch in Zahlen: Nachhaltigkeitsfonds verzeichneten zuletzt drei Jahre in Folge Mittelabflüsse.

Icao erfasst keine Nachhaltigkeitsinitiativen mehr

Parallel dazu sprechen auch Unternehmen seltener über Themen wie Dekarbonisierung oder ESG. In Auswertungen von mehr als 6000 Analystenkonferenzen gingen entsprechende Begriffe zuletzt um über 20 Prozent zurück, zeigt ein aktueller Bericht des Lufthansa Innovation Hub.

Ein ähnlicher Trend ist auch in der Luftfahrt zu beobachten. Laut der International Civil Aviation Organization Icao ist die Zahl konkreter Initiativen von Airlines zur Reduktion von CO₂-Emissionen massiv gesunken, um ganze 96 Prozent. Während 2021 noch rund 50 Projekte gezählt wurden, waren es 2024 weniger als fünf. 2025 stellte die Organisation die Erfassung solcher Initiativen ganz ein.

Emissionen sinken trotzdem

Parallel dazu passen mehrere Fluggesellschaften ihre eigenen Klimaziele an. Als Beispiel nehmen die Autoren Delta Air Lines. Die Fluggesellschaft hat ihr Netto-Null-Ziel für 2050 zuletzt neu eingeordnet. Es gilt jetzt nicht mehr als festes Versprechen, sondern als langfristige Perspektive. Auch ein Zwischenziel, bis 2030 einen Anteil von 10 Prozent nachhaltigem Treibstoff zu erreichen, verschwand aus der Kommunikation. Andere Airlines gehen ähnlich vor, schwächen Formulierungen ab oder verschieben Zeitpläne.

Doch der Eindruck, die Branche entferne sich vom Klimaschutz, greift zu kurz, finden die Autoren. Ein Blick auf die tatsächlichen Emissionen zeigt denn auch ein differenzierteres Bild. Zwischen 2019 und 2025 ist die weltweite Kapazität der Airlines um rund 14 Prozent gewachsen. Die CO₂-Emissionen stiegen im gleichen Zeitraum jedoch nur um etwa 2 Prozent. Das deutet darauf hin, dass Fluggesellschaften deutlich sauberer geworden sind – vor allem durch modernere, sparsamere Flugzeuge.

Steigende Kerosinpreise verringern Preisunterschied zu SAF

Ein weiterer Faktor kommt hinzu: steigende Kerosinpreise. Durch die aktuellen geopolitischen Spannungen hat sich der Preisabstand zwischen herkömmlichem Treibstoff und nachhaltigen Alternativen verkleinert. Und Kerosin dürfte auch bei einer politischen Entspannung noch eine ganze Weile deutlich teurer bleiben. Aktuelle Prognosen der Energiewirtschaft gehen davon aus, dass der Ölpreis 2026 im Schnitt bei rund 86 Dollar pro Barrel liegen könnte – nach etwa 69 Dollar im Jahr zuvor.

Das könnte die Nutzung von Sustainable Aviation Fuel SAF wirtschaftlich attraktiver machen. Denn bisher galt der hohe Preis als größtes Hindernis, neben der sehr knappen Verfügbarkeit. Während das Thema öffentlich an Aufmerksamkeit verliert, entwickelt sich im Hintergrund aber inzwischen immerhin ein eigenes Ökosystem weiter. Spezialisierte Unternehmen arbeiten an Technologien rund um nachhaltige Treibstoffe und bauen ihre Kapazitäten aus.

Weniger laut, aber weiter effektiv

Die große Aufmerksamkeit mag nachgelassen haben. Auch viele Versprechen werden vorsichtiger formuliert. Doch die Zahlen erzählen eine andere Geschichte: Die Branche wird effizienter, Technologien entwickeln sich weiter, und wirtschaftliche Faktoren verschieben die Dynamik. Oder anders gesagt: Die Luftfahrt spricht weniger über Klimaschutz. Aber aufgehört hat sie damit nicht.

Wir lieben Flugzeuge – und guten Journalismus. Unser Team aus erfahrenen Redakteurinnen und Redakteuren recherchiert, prüft, erklärt. text:
The Indian Ladies Association Bahrain has officially launched its 70th year celebrations with a vibrant social media campaign titled The Platinum Power-Up, aimed at reconnecting members and celebrating the spirit that has shaped the association for seven decades.

The campaign, unveiled through a series of engaging digital reels, encourages members to rediscover, recapture, and reignite their sense of belonging while highlighting the talents and contributions of the ILA community over the years.

President Smitha Jensen said the initiative is designed to bring members together ahead of the association’s milestone platinum year celebrations.

“The association is just a building without members’ talent, their voice, presence, and energy,” she said. “Through this fun project, we want to bring members together and rediscover their various talents ahead of our power-packed plans for our Platinum year.”

The association said the 70th year celebrations will feature glamour, entertainment, community engagement, and a range of cultural and social activities reflecting the vibrant spirit of ILA and its members.

Production schedules, locations, and props management are being coordinated by Raka Mukhopadhyay and Minal Virani. Costumes and continuity are being handled by Ranjana Jaiswal and Monika Ameta.

text:
Egypt is advancing efforts to develop a more sustainable aviation sector through investments in green hydrogen and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), Minister of Civil Aviation Sameh El Hefny said during the Egypt Green Hydrogen Forum 2026.

El Hefny participated in the forum, organised by the German Arab Chamber of Industry and Commerce (AHK) in cooperation with the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), as part of the Egyptian-German Green Hydrogen Partnership (GH2P).

The event brought together government officials, international experts, and representatives from the aviation, energy and maritime sectors to discuss the role of green hydrogen and sustainable fuels in reducing carbon emissions.

Speaking during a high-level session titled “Fueling the Future – Green Hydrogen for Maritime and Aviation Fuels,” El Hefny said Egypt is working to accelerate the transition towards lower-emission aviation and expand the adoption of clean energy solutions in line with Egypt Vision 2030.

He noted that green hydrogen and SAF are increasingly becoming central to the future of global transport, adding that the ministry’s strategy focuses on gradually expanding the use of sustainable fuels while reducing the aviation sector’s carbon footprint.

According to the minister, Egypt has already begun implementing several sustainability initiatives, including increasing the use of solar energy at airports and coordinating with the ministries of petroleum and electricity to encourage investment in SAF production.

El Hefny also revealed that the civil aviation sector is studying plans to establish a new SAF production facility as part of wider efforts to localise low-emission aviation industries and support technology transfer.

He added that Egypt’s strategic geographic location, infrastructure and renewable energy resources position the country to become a regional hub for green hydrogen and sustainable aviation fuel production.

The minister further stressed Egypt’s commitment to implementing environmental standards issued by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) as part of efforts to align the sector with global sustainability requirements.

On the sidelines of the forum, the tourism and aviation committee at the German Arab Chamber of Industry and Commerce held talks with El Hefny on potential cooperation in tourism and aviation, including airport development, improving passenger experience, and strengthening Egypt’s competitiveness as a tourism destination.

title: Topsoe's pilot reactor ran on two different carbon sources at once and still produced stable ...
description:
Making synthetic aviation fuel requires two things at once: a steady carbon feedstock and cheap renewable electricity.
The output was stable syncrude, consistently suited for refining into sustainable aviation fuel.
This built-in flexibility means a synthetic fuel plant isn’t just a passive electricity consumer.
From Syncrude to Sustainable Aviation Fuel The pilot didn’t stop at syngas.
Publication in the Journal of CO2 Utilization represents a documented, peer-reviewed milestone for flexible synthetic fuel production.
text:
Making synthetic aviation fuel requires two things at once: a steady carbon feedstock and cheap renewable electricity. In practice, neither shows up on schedule.

In a pilot-scale experiment published in the Journal of CO2 Utilization, Topsoe scientists fed two entirely different carbon sources — CO2 and biogas — into the same reactor, sometimes simultaneously, sometimes in sequence. The output was stable syncrude, consistently suited for refining into sustainable aviation fuel.

The Carbon-Sourcing Problem Holding E-Fuels Back

Synthetic fuels are widely viewed as one of the few credible pathways to decarbonizing aviation, where direct electrification isn’t an option. But scaling up production has run into a persistent structural problem: most e-fuel processes are built around a single carbon source, typically CO2, and that dependency creates real vulnerability. Supply disruptions, fluctuating renewable electricity prices, and inconsistent feedstock availability can all stall output at exactly the wrong moment.

The FrontFuel initiative was designed to confront these constraints directly. Sponsored by Denmark’s Energy Technology Development and Demonstration Program (EUDP) and led by researchers from Topsoe, Aarhus University, and Sasol, the project set out to demonstrate whether pilot-scale synthetic fuel production could be made genuinely flexible — not just in theory, but in a working reactor system producing fuel-grade output.

A Reactor That Switches Between Feedstocks on the Fly

The technical centerpiece of the study is Topsoe’s eREACT™ technology, which enabled two chemically distinct processes to run interchangeably inside the same reactor unit. Steam reforming of biogas (CH4) and reverse water-gas shift of CO2 and hydrogen aren’t the same reaction. Yet the system handled both — and transitions between them — without requiring a separate apparatus for each.

What made this possible was dynamic control of the feed gas composition using hydrogen and steam. As the ratio of CO2 to CH4 at the reactor inlet varied, operators adjusted these inputs to keep the syngas output at a constant composition, producing stable syncrude throughout the experiment even as the feedstock mix changed. Flexibility, in other words, didn’t come at the cost of consistency.

That stability matters more than it might first appear. Downstream fuel synthesis processes are sensitive to syngas quality, so any instability at the reforming stage propagates through the entire production chain. The pilot maintaining steady output across different feedstock conditions is a meaningful proof of concept — not an incremental refinement.

Turning Grid Volatility Into a Production Advantage

One of the less obvious implications of this dual-feedstock capability is what it means for how a facility interacts with the electrical grid. Converting CO2 is more energy-intensive than converting biogas — a difference that might look like a complication but is actually a lever.

When renewable electricity is cheap and abundant, during peak wind or solar generation, a plant can lean heavily on CO2 conversion, consuming more power and helping absorb grid surplus. When electricity is scarce and expensive, the same facility can shift toward the less energy-intensive biogas pathway, reducing its draw on the grid without halting production. The switching happens within the same system, with no retooling required.

This built-in flexibility means a synthetic fuel plant isn’t just a passive electricity consumer. It can act as a flexible load, actively supporting grid balance. The same logic applies to natural fluctuations in feedstock availability: if CO2 supply tightens or biogas delivery is interrupted, the system compensates rather than shuts down.

From Syncrude to Sustainable Aviation Fuel

The pilot didn’t stop at syngas. Syncrude produced by the eREACT system was routed through Sasol’s Fischer-Tropsch technology, and the output was confirmed to be of a quality suitable for upgrading into sustainable aviation fuel. That full-chain result — from mixed carbon feedstocks through to SAF-grade syncrude — is what gives the study its weight.

The setup also allows byproducts from downstream fuel synthesis to be recycled back into the eREACT system, improving overall yield and cutting waste. At commercial scale, where efficiency losses compound quickly, that kind of integration isn’t a nice-to-have.

Publication in the Journal of CO2 Utilization represents a documented, peer-reviewed milestone for flexible synthetic fuel production. Pilot scale is not commercial scale, and the path from one to the other involves substantial engineering, financing, and regulatory work. But the FrontFuel results give producers and policymakers something concrete to build on: a demonstrated system that handles variable carbon inputs, supports grid stability, and still delivers aviation-grade output. The next question is how quickly that architecture can be replicated at the scale aviation actually needs.

Utopia, which holds a majority stake in Wakud International—Oman’s first dedicated biodiesel refinery—aims to enhance production of next-generation sustainable biofuels. This initiative aligns with Oman Vision 2040’s objectives focused on industrial innovation and economic diversification.

Faris al Kharusi, CEO of UWI, emphasized the attractive conditions for biofuel production, stating, “The solar density, abundance of appropriate salinity water, and collaboration with both public and private partners position HutanBio as a crucial local content generator in the biochain.”

As part of this agreement, Wakud will serve as an offtaker, allowing both companies to scale operations simultaneously and establish a solid foundation for the production and distribution of low-carbon fuels.

Project stakeholders have noted Oman’s favorable geographical and industrial attributes as critical to this collaboration. The Sultanate’s high solar radiation, extensive coastline, and access to saline water create an optimal environment for coastal aquaculture and algae farming. Integrating this technology with Oman’s established oil and gas framework further solidifies the country’s position as a potential leader in the sustainable fuels market.

Omani scientist Aziza al Mughairy remarked, “HutanBio’s initiative could elevate Oman as a regional pioneer in next-generation biofuels, enhancing the Sultanate’s contribution to global decarbonization and food security while supporting economic diversification and green innovation in line with Oman Vision 2040.”

The first deployment is planned for late 2027, followed by significant expansion to meet the demands of the aviation and maritime sectors. By leveraging Oman’s arid coastlines and existing refinery facilities, the partnership between HutanBio and Wakud aims to transform non-arable land into a cutting-edge biofuel hub, propelling decarbonization in these vital industries.

BUSINESS REPORTER

MUSCAT, MAY 17

In a move designed to reinforce the Sultanate of Oman’s position within the global green economy, UK-based biotechnology firm HutanBio has entered into a strategic Memorandum of Understanding with Oman’s Utopia World Investment (UWI) to support the growth of a sustainable fuels sector in Oman.

Utopia is a majority shareholder in Wakud International, which owns and operates Oman’s first dedicated biodiesel refinery. The collaboration seeks to develop and scale next-generation sustainable biofuel production, directly supporting the industrial innovation and economic diversification goals outlined in Oman Vision 2040.

Faris al Kharusi, CEO of UWI, shared, “Solar density conditions, abundance of water with appropriate salinity ranges and development with partners both public and private allow HuntanBio to be strategically placed as an economic local content generator in the biochain”.

The partnership centres on the commercialisation of HutanBio’s proprietary algae-based oil technology, regarded as a scientific breakthrough for its proven ability to harness a newly discovered genus of algae identified by Dr John Archer of Cambridge University.

Under the terms of the agreement, Wakud will act as an offtaker as both entities scale their operations simultaneously, creating a robust framework for the domestic production and deployment of low-carbon fuels. This initiative arrives at a critical juncture for the aviation industry, which currently utilises less than 0.5% sustainable aviation fuel despite aggressive long-term decarbonisation targets of 25%. This localised biotechnology initiative has the potential to simultaneously enhance food security, as the second byproduct, aside from the biofuel, is protein-rich biomass.

Beyond its environmental impact, the project is expected to stimulate the growth of a specialised biotechnology industry in Oman, generating skilled employment opportunities and fostering local research and development capabilities. Following successful discussions with government representatives and industry leaders, Manshu Agarwal, CEO of HutanBio, said the partnership reflects a shared ambition to position Oman at the forefront of the global clean energy transition.

“Oman is perhaps the single best place on Earth to build and scale this project, particularly because of its geopolitical stability, excellent human capital and refinery infrastructure in oil and gas; and of course the ideal climate for growing this algae”, he stated.

Significantly, the technology underpinning this venture is the result of over a decade of research led by Dr John Archer, whose distinguished career includes leadership roles at Cambridge, MIT and being one of the founders of KAUST’s biology department. HutanBio’s novel microalgae strain demonstrates significantly higher productivity than conventional varieties, offering a potential path to producing sustainable crude alternatives at cost parity with traditional fossil fuels.

Project stakeholders have highlighted Oman’s unique geographical and industrial profile as a primary driver for this collaboration. The Sultanate of Oman’s exceptionally high solar radiation, extensive coastline and access to saline water provide an ideal environment for coastal aquaculture and algae cultivation. Furthermore, the ability to integrate this technology into Oman’s established oil and gas infrastructure and utilise its political stability makes the country a premier candidate for global leadership in the sustainable fuels sector.

Omani scientist Aziza al Mughairy added: “HutanBio’s initiative could position Oman as a regional leader in next-generation biofuels, strengthening the Sultanate of Oman’s contribution to global decarbonisation and food security efforts while supporting economic diversification, green innovation and the objectives of Oman Vision 2040 on several fronts”.

The first site is set to deploy in late 2027, before a massive scale expansion that can cover the needs of the entire aviation and maritime industry. By utilising Oman's arid coastlines and existing refinery infrastructure, the HutanBio and Wakud partnership transforms non-arable land into a high-tech biofuel hub that drives decarbonisation in the aviation and maritime sectors.

text:
Tarn Nicholls is gearing up to launch the space on May 25

A young boxer who tragically lost his dad to cancer has poured his energies into building a community gym in the village of North Somercotes. Tarn Nicholls has spent the last six weeks transforming an empty former slaughterhouse into an "old school" boxing gym which he hopes will inspire young people and adults in the area.

The 22 year-old, who was formerly a builder, was introduced to the sport by his dad who died in December last year. Having stopped boxing to care for his dad, Tarn was encouraged to start training again by his wife.

It led to an idea that the bouncer could create his own "spit and sawdust" space on a budget. And soon he sought out the empty unit on Keeling Street which runs through the centre of the East Lindsey village, in an area where Tarn says there are few boxing facilities.

He explained: "It's really something for me to do - to keep me sane - and also its there for the community."

He added: "In the village of North Somercotes there's not an awful lot for the kids, or for anyone. But it'll be good particularly for the kids to get into the gym and learn new skills."

In his fighting days, Tarn was successful in winning belts in matches not sanctioned by the British Boxing Board. He became friends with retired professional boxer Joe Egan, a multiple winner of Irish Heavyweight Boxing titles and once a regular sparring partner of heavyweight giant Mike Tyson.

With a number of similar contacts in the boxing world, Tarn hopes to stage an opening event on Monday, May 25 with locals and others encouraged to visit the gym from 12noon onwards to try their hands at the sport.

Now, having handed in his notice as a doorman, Tarn will turn his attentions full time to the gym - called Nicholls Boxing - which will offer mainly classes to beginners and experienced fighters. Inside, the venue features multiple punchbags, weights and a ring - which is due to be delivered in the coming days.

Classes will centre around boxing-focussed circuits and exercises - most led by Tarn himself with some help from wife, Leah. A youth class for children and young people aged eight-16 is programmed between 4pm-5pm, with an adult class after that, and from 7pm-8pm an open gym for anyone to train under their own steam.

On Tuesdays and Thursdays, a "Little Warriors" class will offer four-eight year-olds a chance to try the sport. And on Thursday evenings a dedicated women's session will take place.

A huge effort has gone into renovating the space with Tarn using his own building skills and friends lending a hand. He hopes that once open, the gym can inspire discipline and confidence among young people in the area and be used for community outreach projects.

He added: "I just recently hung up the bags and the transformation from an empty warehouse into something that resembles a gym is just amazing."

text:
The company is going all-out for the British Heart Foundation

A family firm in Immingham is honouring the memory of its “kind and caring” founder by pledging to raise £100,000 for the British Heart Foundation through a series of events and challenges. APM Commercials, which specialises in haulage trailer repairs, sales and rentals was set up 35 years ago by Steve Gilboy and his wife Marie, who spotted that the growing international port needed the services of a trailer maintenance business.

Steve, a father of four and grandfather of nine, who was known fondly by family and his staff as “Gilly”, sadly died in September 2023 from a cardiac arrest that happened while at home in bed. Two years previously he had suffered a heart attack; he underwent a procedure to be fitted with two stents and was prescribed medication.

The firm, which employs 44 people, was built on Steve and Marie’s strong family values of fairness, attention to detail and excellent customer service. Today, the Gilboys’ three sons, Andrew, Patrick and Mike together with their wives are all directors at the firm and Marie, 67, remains a member of the board.

Steve’s daughter-in-law Chloe Gilboy, who is head of HR, said: “Steve was a big character, and his personality filled the room. He was funny, kind and caring and always had great stories to tell.

“He was so loved by all of us who work here and he loved everyone in return. His presence is still very much part of the business.

“We have his photos around the office and a quote of his on the wall to inspire us daily. When we have decisions to make, we always ask ourselves, what would dad do? What would Gilly say now?

“We are determined as a family and as a business to honour him through fundraising for the BHF and we have set a big target of £100,000 because we know it’s possible and we know how proud he would be of us all.” The firm has already held two golf days at Laceby Manor, near Grimsby, raising nearly £15,000, and Mike has taken part in a white-collar boxing event raising £1,350.

Andrew and Patrick together with their partners, Zoe and Shermille and cousin Dominic, completed the BHF’s London to Brighton Bike Ride in June last year and raised £1,700. A curry night hosted by Abdul’s Kitchen, in Ulceby, raised a further £1,300.

Chloe said: “With lots more fundraising in place for 2026 and 2027, including another BHF London to Brighton Bike ride, Gilly’s Annual Golf Day, a sky dive and then the Manchester Marathon booked for 2027, we aim to be another step closer to our target.” Melanie Meik, fundraising manager for BHF, said: “We are so grateful to the Gilboy family and everyone at APM Commercials for choosing to raise funds for the British Heart Foundation in honour of Steve and in recognition of the lifesaving research BHF funds throughout the UK.

“It is so abundantly clear how inspirational Steve was and always will be to this very special family business. His memory and everything he stood for is inspiring his loyal team and loving family to help the BHF power groundbreaking cardiovascular research to save and improve lives, bring hope to families, and keep hearts beating across the UK.”

For more information about the charity, visit bhf.org.uk and you can donate to the Steve ‘Gilly’ Gilboy fundraising via the BHF website here.

title: Transformasi Sawit Nasional Bangkitkan Energi Indonesia Masa Depan Berkelanjutan
description:
Menurut beliau, sawit tidak boleh lagi hanya dipandang sebagai komoditas ekspor mentah, tetapi harus menjadi pusat transformasi ekonomi hijau Indonesia.
Yang paling menarik dan sangat inspiratif, Dr. Endy menempatkan kampus vokasi sebagai motor penggerak transformasi nasional.
Kampus vokasi perlu membangun teaching factory biofuel, mini biodiesel plant, laboratorium energi terbarukan, pilot plant oleokimia, smart energy laboratory, hingga inkubator startup energi hijau.
Tidak hanya itu, beliau juga menekankan pentingnya penguatan UMKM hijau berbasis sawit dan ekonomi sirkular.
Selama Indonesia masih bergantung pada impor energi, impor bahan baku, dan impor teknologi, maka setiap krisis global akan terus menjadi ancaman besar bagi ekonomi nasional.
text:
Di tengah gejolak pelemahan rupiah global, kenaikan harga energi dunia, hingga ancaman perlambatan ekonomi internasional, muncul satu kajian visioner yang sangat menarik, futuristik, sekaligus membangkitkan optimisme besar bagi masa depan Indonesia. Kajian tersebut datang dari Dr. Mohamad Endy Julianto, dosen TRKI Vokasi UNDIP sekaligus konsultan industri yang aktif mengkaji transformasi energi nasional, hilirisasi industri hijau, bioenergi, serta penguatan ketahanan ekonomi berbasis sumber daya lokal Indonesia.

Dalam pandangannya yang sangat strategis, Dr. Endy menegaskan bahwa pelemahan rupiah bukan sekadar persoalan kurs atau angka ekonomi di layar bursa, tetapi merupakan alarm nasional tentang masih besarnya ketergantungan Indonesia terhadap impor energi, bahan baku industri, hingga teknologi luar negeri. Ketika rupiah melemah menembus Rp16.000 per dolar AS, dampaknya terasa seperti efek domino raksasa: impor minyak mentah melonjak, subsidi energi membengkak, harga logistik meningkat, biaya industri naik, daya beli masyarakat melemah, dan UMKM ikut tertekan. Menurut beliau, selama Indonesia masih sangat tergantung pada energi fosil impor dan transaksi global berbasis dolar, maka gejolak ekonomi dunia akan terus mudah mengguncang stabilitas nasional.

Namun yang paling mengagumkan, kajian Dr. Endy tidak berhenti pada kritik persoalan. Justru dari tantangan global tersebut lahir gagasan besar tentang bagaimana Indonesia harus melakukan lompatan strategis menuju negara industri hijau yang mandiri energi melalui kolaborasi pemerintah, kampus, industri, UMKM, dan masyarakat dengan memanfaatkan kekuatan sawit dan turunannya sebagai fondasi masa depan energi nasional.

Menurut beliau, sawit tidak boleh lagi hanya dipandang sebagai komoditas ekspor mentah, tetapi harus menjadi pusat transformasi ekonomi hijau Indonesia. Indonesia memiliki potensi luar biasa melalui biodiesel, green diesel, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), biomassa sawit, biogas POME, biochar, bioplastik berbasis lignoselulosa sawit, hingga produk oleokimia bernilai tinggi yang mampu mengurangi ketergantungan impor energi dan bahan baku kimia industri. Program pemerintah seperti B35 menuju B40 hingga B50 dinilai sebagai langkah sangat strategis dalam menjaga stabilitas energi nasional sekaligus mengurangi tekanan impor BBM berbasis dolar.

Lebih jauh lagi, Dr. Endy menilai masa depan industri sawit Indonesia harus bergerak menuju advanced downstream industry melalui pengembangan green surfactant, green solvent, gliserol bernilai tinggi, biofuel generasi lanjut, material maju berbasis biomassa sawit, hingga biopolimer ramah lingkungan. Dengan hilirisasi yang kuat, Indonesia tidak lagi hanya menjadi eksportir bahan mentah, tetapi mampu naik kelas menjadi produsen teknologi hijau dunia dengan nilai tambah tinggi.

Sebagai konsultan industri, beliau juga menyoroti pentingnya perubahan paradigma industri nasional. Industri Indonesia harus berubah dari sekadar "high energy consumer" menjadi "smart green industry" yang menerapkan efisiensi energi, circular economy, rooftop solar, smart manufacturing, waste-to-energy, dan pemanfaatan biomassa sawit sebagai sumber energi alternatif murah dan berkelanjutan. Menurutnya, transformasi industri hijau bukan lagi pilihan, tetapi kebutuhan mutlak untuk menghadapi kompetisi global masa depan.

Yang paling menarik dan sangat inspiratif, Dr. Endy menempatkan kampus vokasi sebagai motor penggerak transformasi nasional. Kampus tidak boleh hanya menjadi pencetak ijazah, tetapi harus menjadi pusat solusi industri dan ketahanan bangsa. Kampus vokasi perlu membangun teaching factory biofuel, mini biodiesel plant, laboratorium energi terbarukan, pilot plant oleokimia, smart energy laboratory, hingga inkubator startup energi hijau. Mahasiswa harus dilatih langsung menyelesaikan persoalan nyata industri dan masyarakat, mulai dari audit energi, efisiensi proses, teknologi biofuel, hingga pengembangan alat tepat guna murah untuk desa dan UMKM.

Tidak hanya itu, beliau juga menekankan pentingnya penguatan UMKM hijau berbasis sawit dan ekonomi sirkular. UMKM Indonesia dinilai memiliki peluang besar masuk ke industri kemasan biodegradable, pupuk organik biomassa, bioenergi skala kecil, hingga produk turunan sawit ramah lingkungan. Dengan dukungan digitalisasi, riset kampus, dan kebijakan pemerintah, UMKM Indonesia diyakini mampu naik kelas menjadi bagian penting rantai pasok industri hijau nasional.

Dalam perspektif kebangsaan, Dr. Endy menegaskan bahwa persoalan energi dan pelemahan rupiah sejatinya adalah persoalan kedaulatan nasional. Selama Indonesia masih bergantung pada impor energi, impor bahan baku, dan impor teknologi, maka setiap krisis global akan terus menjadi ancaman besar bagi ekonomi nasional. Karena itu, momentum krisis harus dijadikan titik lompatan besar menuju Indonesia yang lebih mandiri, lebih hijau, lebih inovatif, dan lebih tangguh menghadapi masa depan dunia.

Dari ruang laboratorium vokasi hingga forum konsultasi industri nasional, gagasan besar itu terus digaungkan oleh Dr. Endy: masa depan Indonesia tidak boleh dibangun di atas ketergantungan, tetapi harus dibangun melalui inovasi, hilirisasi sawit, efisiensi energi, kolaborasi lintas sektor, dan keberanian melakukan transformasi besar bangsa menuju Indonesia hijau, mandiri energi, dan berdaya saing global.

title: From Kigali to Nairobi: Can Africa rise beyond its shadows? - TheCable
description:
The Africa Forward Summit in Nairobi, co-hosted by Kenyan President William Ruto and French President Emmanuel Macron, focused on attracting foreign capital and partnerships.
At the same time, the Africa CEO Forum in Kigali, backed by Rwandan President Paul Kagame, emphasised African agency and the urgent need for continental scale.
In sharp contrast, the Kigali Africa CEO Forum 2026, themed Scale or Fail: Why Africa Must Embrace Shared Ownership, placed the African private sector at the centre.
Furthermore, bilateral arrangements risk undermining the African Continental Free Trade Area by creating special advantages for external firms over African competitors.
One path relies on rapid inflows of foreign capital, even if it means external firms lead project execution.
text:
BY SHOLA ADEBOWALE

In the space of just 72 hours in May 2026, two contrasting visions for Africa’s economic future unfolded barely one hour’s flight apart. The Africa Forward Summit in Nairobi, co-hosted by Kenyan President William Ruto and French President Emmanuel Macron, focused on attracting foreign capital and partnerships. At the same time, the Africa CEO Forum in Kigali, backed by Rwandan President Paul Kagame, emphasised African agency and the urgent need for continental scale. The close timing of these events brought a fundamental question into sharp focus: can Africa successfully combine foreign partnerships with homegrown ownership to break free from historical cycles of dependence, or will it remain caught between short-term gains and long-term unfulfilled potential?

The Nairobi summit promoted a renewed partnership with France, shifting the narrative from aid to co-investment. Announcements at the event included around $27 billion in deals spanning clean energy, artificial intelligence, agriculture, infrastructure, and aviation. A major highlight was the agreement between Kenya Airways and Rubis Energy to develop a sustainable aviation fuel plant near Nairobi. For France, the summit formed part of a strategic effort to rebuild economic influence after losing ground in the Sahel. For Kenya and other participating African countries, it represented an opportunity to secure capital for green industrial projects and job creation.

In sharp contrast, the Kigali Africa CEO Forum 2026, themed Scale or Fail: Why Africa Must Embrace Shared Ownership, placed the African private sector at the centre. The gathering attracted more than 2,800 CEOs, investors, and several heads of state without any single foreign power dominating the conversation. Discussions focused on mobilising African capital from pension funds, banks, and stock exchanges to build large-scale continental champions in sectors such as telecoms, logistics, pharmaceuticals, and energy. Speakers, including President Kagame, stressed the importance of owning strategic value chains, noting that Africa possesses vast solar potential and most of the world’s battery minerals. Attention also turned to practical tools for integration, including the African Continental Free Trade Area, the Lobito Corridor, the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System, and legal harmonisation initiatives.

The gains from the Nairobi approach are immediate and tangible. The 27 billion dollars in commitments offer much-needed capital to close infrastructure gaps. The sustainable aviation fuel project, for instance, could reduce airline costs, cut emissions, generate employment, and help position East Africa in the growing low-carbon fuel market. Partnerships with French companies bring valuable technology and expertise in solar power, hydropower, and clean cooking solutions, creating potential learning opportunities for African engineers and firms. In addition, France’s active courtship gives African governments greater negotiating leverage than in previous decades.

The advantages of the Kigali forum are more structural and long-term. By encouraging shared ownership, the event pushed African institutional investors to move beyond conservative government bonds and begin financing scalable African enterprises. Success in this direction could lead to the emergence of more homegrown conglomerates with the financial strength to compete across borders and eventually on the global stage. The forum also highlighted the need for deeper regional integration to reduce the high transaction costs that have kept African markets fragmented and small. Most importantly, greater ownership of value chains would allow Africa to capture more jobs, profits, and economic multipliers instead of exporting raw materials and importing finished goods at higher prices.

Yet both approaches carry significant risks. The Nairobi model risks deepening dependency if contracts heavily favour foreign suppliers and equipment, allowing profits to flow back abroad with limited local industrialisation. Political expectations tied to these deals, whether around security cooperation or diplomatic alignment, could also conflict with broader African interests. Furthermore, bilateral arrangements risk undermining the African Continental Free Trade Area by creating special advantages for external firms over African competitors.

The Kigali vision faces its own challenges. African pension funds and banks have historically been risk-averse, and it remains uncertain whether they will commit capital at the required scale. There is also the danger of elite capture, where benefits flow mainly to a few large players and connected interests, leaving small and medium enterprises as well as smaller economies behind. Above all, the persistent gap between ambitious declarations and actual implementation threatens to turn the shared ownership agenda into another set of unfulfilled promises, especially given slow progress on customs reform, non-tariff barriers, and transport infrastructure.

Taken together, these two summits illustrate the two paths Africa is currently navigating. One path relies on rapid inflows of foreign capital, even if it means external firms lead project execution. This approach delivers quick infrastructure wins, job creation, and a strong signal that Africa is open for business. However, it carries the danger of losing control over strategic sectors and locking the continent into supplier-customer relationships that limit deeper industrialisation. The second path focuses on building African-owned scale through regional integration and internal capital mobilisation. Though slower and more demanding, it promises greater value retention and stronger African firms over time.

The most effective strategy lies in using the first path to accelerate the second. Africa should accept foreign capital for critical projects in energy and aviation while insisting on meaningful African equity participation, local content requirements, skills transfer, and genuine technology sharing from the beginning. Deals must be structured so that African firms gradually take larger roles in subsequent phases. In this way, external resources help build the infrastructure and capabilities needed for continental champions to emerge and compete.

Nairobi provided Africa with fresh capital and European attention. Kigali offered a clearer roadmap for reducing dependence on such inflows in the future. If both are pursued with discipline and strategic coherence, the continent stands to win by blending external capital with internal scale to create industries that are African-owned and globally competitive. If not, the risk is more debt, continued import dependence, and the same familiar story repeating in 2030: enormous potential discussed, but rarely captured.

The next 24 months will reveal which direction gains real traction. Africa does not lack resources or ambition. What will ultimately decide the outcome is the quality of execution, the strength of negotiation, and the consistency between opportunistic partnerships and a long-term vision of genuine economic sovereignty.
